question: In adults whose ankle fracture was reduced in ED, was the check X-ray reviewed and the reduction documented as adequate before they left ED?
why: Poor ED reduction leads to skin compromise and repeat manipulations. Corpus: [1235] improved 'adequacy of reduction' by 25% with an ED algorithm, but no audit measured this single BOAST item on its own.

standard.source: BOAST The Management of Ankle Fractures (BOA, August 2016), Standards for Practice
standard.wording: Adequate reduction must be confirmed by review of repeat radiographs and documented before transfer from ED.

population: Include: adults (skeletally mature) with a closed malleolar or syndesmotic ankle fracture reduced in ED. Exclude: pilon, open fractures, children, reductions done only in theatre.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 6 months (fewer in small units: take all).
data_source: ED system (departure time, reduction note); PACS (post-reduction image time); orthopaedic clerking.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
Secondary: BOAST says must be repeated and documented

change: Add a mandatory 'post-reduction X-ray reviewed: adequate / not adequate, by whom' line to the ED ankle reduction procedure note (EPR template), which must be completed before the ED discharge/transfer step.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive reduced ankle fractures, same template.
close_loop: Present at joint ED/T&O governance. If it works, make the template field mandatory in the ED procedure record and add it to the ED induction pack.
evidence: [1235] Scunthorpe: adequacy of reduction improved by 25%, whole-leg films +60% (ED poster algorithm plus ortho attending after a failed reduction)
[1659] single centre UK: repeat neurovascular and skin documentation rose after education (documentation of ankle fractures, education only)
[1569] Aintree MTC: malreduction after fixation 33% → 2.4% (process change plus education)
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients (ED record plus PACS timestamps)
pass: A post-reduction radiograph exists on PACS with a time before the ED departure time, AND the notes contain an entry reviewing it (adequate / not adequate) timed before departure.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In adults with an ankle fracture of uncertain stability treated in a cast or boot, was a repeat X-ray (weight-bearing if possible) done within 2 weeks of injury?
why: Uncertain-stability fractures can displace unseen; late displacement changes treatment. Corpus ankle audits focus on documentation, fixation and syndesmosis ([1659], [1230]); none measured the 2-week check film.

standard.source: BOAST The Management of Ankle Fractures (BOA, August 2016); also NICE NG38 rec 1.4.1 (2016)
standard.wording: In fracture patterns where stability is uncertain, patients should be reviewed within 2 weeks with further radiographs (weight bearing if possible) to confirm the position remains acceptable.

population: Include: adults with a closed ankle fracture treated non-operatively where the clinic or virtual fracture clinic (VFC) note says stability is uncertain (for example isolated Weber B with no medial clear-space widening on non-weight-bearing films). Exclude: fractures judged clearly stable or clearly unstable, and patients listed for surgery at first review.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients from VFC/fracture clinic lists over the last 4–6 months.
data_source: VFC outcome notes; PACS dates and view labels (weight-bearing marker); fracture clinic letters.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Add a VFC outcome button 'Uncertain stability: weight-bearing mortise and lateral X-ray at 10–14 days' that books the X-ray and clinic slot automatically.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 40 consecutive eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at T&O audit meeting and to VFC team; embed the booking button and the weight-bearing radiograph request code in the radiology order set.
evidence: [1427] Blackburn fracture clinic: functional treatment of stable ankle fractures rarely followed → progressive improvement with fewer check films (departmental guideline)
[1538] DGH: 6% seen within 72 h → 100% (virtual fracture clinic, system change)
[1448] A&E: protocol completion 87% and 53% fewer inappropriate referrals (ankle injury protocol)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from VFC list plus PACS
pass: A repeat ankle radiograph dated ≤14 days after injury. Record separately whether it was weight-bearing.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In patients with a suspected Achilles tendon rupture, was a definitive treatment plan (surgery or a named non-operative protocol) documented within 72 hours of first presentation?
why: Delays to ultrasound and to a treatment decision are common: [1669] 34.5% had a plan within one week; [1626] 83% within two weeks. The February 2026 BOAST sets a new, tighter 72-hour standard that no corpus audit has measured.

standard.source: BOAST Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026)
standard.wording: A definitive treatment plan should be documented for all patients within 72 hours of first presentation and copied to the patient and their GP.

population: Include: adults coded or referred to VFC/fracture clinic with suspected acute Achilles tendon rupture. Exclude: re-ruptures already under follow-up, injuries more than 2 weeks old at presentation.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 6–9 months (all cases if fewer).
data_source: ED system (arrival time); VFC/fracture clinic notes (plan time); radiology system (ultrasound request/scan dates if used).

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: A single ED/VFC Achilles pathway sheet: equinus boot at ED, direct VFC referral flagged 'Achilles', and consultant plan at the next-day trauma meeting (no routine wait for ultrasound where clinical tests are clear).
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 (extend to 3 months if case numbers are low), next 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at T&O and ED governance; if it works, make the Achilles pathway sheet part of the ED order set and VFC template.
evidence: [1669] DGH VFC: plan within 1 week 34.5% → 74.2% (other professionals allowed to start investigations, system change)
[1730] Dorset: ultrasound within 14 days 43% → 59%, boot use 80% → 86% (posters plus a new 'Ultrasound Achilles' request code)
[1626] Portsmouth: 83% decision within 2 weeks; revised pathway written, not re-audited
pass: A documented definitive plan (operative, or non-operative with a named boot/wedge protocol) timed ≤72 hours after first ED/UTC arrival.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In patients discharged in a boot or cast for an Achilles tendon rupture, was a VTE risk assessment documented at first contact?
why: Achilles ruptures are a high VTE risk group and immobilisation is long. Lower-limb cast VTE audits exist ([1228], [1358]) but none looked at Achilles ruptures alone against the new 2026 BOAST wording.

standard.source: BOAST Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026); links to NICE NG89 rec 1.11.1 (2018)
standard.wording: A documented risk assessment for venous thromboembolism (VTE) should be conducted for all patients with a lower limb injury. (NICE NG89)

population: Include: adults with suspected or confirmed Achilles tendon rupture discharged in a boot or cast. Exclude: patients already on therapeutic anticoagulation, patients admitted.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 6–9 months.
data_source: ED record/VTE form; drug chart or discharge prescription (LMWH/DOAC); fracture clinic notes.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Build the lower-limb immobilisation VTE tool into the ED discharge step so the boot/cast discharge cannot be completed without it (hard stop).
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 (or 3 months for numbers), next 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED and T&O governance and the trust thrombosis committee; if it works, extend the hard stop to all lower-limb casts.
evidence: [1358] Stockport ED: documented VTE assessment 32% → 93.1% (pathway redesign with electronic discharge prompt/block)
[1228] Harrogate ED: 45% → 78% (VTE section added to VFC booking form, then posters and forms in boots)
[1730] Dorset Achilles pathway: VTE prophylaxis 80% → 80.5% (posters and email only, no change)
pass: A completed VTE risk assessment (tool or free text weighing VTE against bleeding risk) in the ED/UTC or first fracture clinic record, dated the day of first presentation.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In adults whose dorsally displaced distal radius fracture was manipulated in ED, was the manipulation done under regional anaesthesia (for example Bier's block) rather than a haematoma block?
why: Haematoma blocks give poorer analgesia and more failed reductions. Corpus has Bier's block documentation audits ([1245]) and analgesia audits ([1292]) but none measured the anaesthetic technique used against BOAST.

standard.source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (BOA, December 2017); also NICE NG38 rec 1.3.1 (2016)
standard.wording: If manipulation is indicated, it should be undertaken using regional anaesthesia, performed by a suitably qualified and trained practitioner (as opposed to local haematoma block).

population: Include: adults (skeletally mature) with a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture manipulated in ED. Exclude: manipulation in theatre, children.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: ED procedure notes; ED drug chart (prilocaine / local anaesthetic); PACS (pre/post images).

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Stock a ready-made Bier's block pack in ED resus with a one-page procedure checklist, and put 'Bier's block' as the default option in the ED distal radius reduction template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and T&O audit; if it works, add Bier's block sign-off to ED registrar competencies and keep the pack on the resus checklist.
evidence: [1305] Oxford ED: operative reduction rate 24.1% → 17.3% (three ED training sessions on BOAST, finger traps and moulding)
[1245] ED/fracture clinic: neurovascular check before Bier's block 34% → 60.3% (intervention not described)
pass: The procedure note records intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block) or another regional block (for example axillary/supraclavicular). Haematoma block, sedation only or gas and air alone = fail.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In patients aged 50 or over with a low-energy distal radius fracture, was a referral to the fracture liaison service (or a documented bone health and falls assessment) made?
why: A wrist fracture is often the first fragility fracture. Bone protection audits in the corpus are mostly about hip fractures; the only wrist loop is old ([1414]: 0% → 81%).

standard.source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (BOA, December 2017)
standard.wording: Patients should be assessed for falls risks and bone health, and referred to the fracture liaison services and or falls service where appropriate.

population: Include: patients aged ≥50 with a low-energy (standing height or less) distal radius fracture. Exclude: high-energy injury, already on FLS follow-up or bone treatment started in the last year.
sample: 50 consecutive patients over the last 3 months.
data_source: VFC/fracture clinic letters; FLS referral log; GP letters; drug history.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Automatic FLS feed: VFC coding of 'distal radius fracture, age ≥50' triggers an electronic referral to the FLS, with an opt-out box.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 50 consecutive patients, same template.
close_loop: Present to T&O, FLS and falls teams; if it works, keep the automatic feed and report monthly FLS capture to the trust.
evidence: [1414] Manchester: distal radius patients investigated/treated/referred 0% → 81% (practice change, not specified)
[1265] VFC: only 37% of stable distal radius fractures mobilised early (single cycle; shows VFC is the right place for a trigger)
pass: An FLS referral, or a documented bone health and falls assessment with a stated outcome, within 12 weeks of injury.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In adults with a distal radius fracture treated in a cast, was an X-ray at cast removal avoided when there was no documented clinical concern?
why: Routine out-of-cast films add radiation, time and clinic visits with no benefit. No audit in corpus measured this BOAST item.

standard.source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (BOA, December 2017)
standard.wording: A radiograph of the patient’s wrist at the time of removing immobilisation is not required unless there is clinical cause for concern.

population: Include: adults with a distal radius fracture treated non-operatively in a cast. Exclude: operative fixation, children.
sample: 50 consecutive patients reaching cast removal over the last 3 months.
data_source: Fracture clinic notes; PACS (X-ray on cast-removal date); clinic outcome.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Change the fracture clinic booking template so 'X-ray on arrival' is no longer the default for distal radius cast-removal visits; the clinician must request it with a reason.
close_loop: Present at T&O audit and to radiology; if it works, remove the default request in the clinic template for good and report X-rays saved.
evidence: [1427] Blackburn: fewer routine check radiographs without loss of safety (departmental guideline, stable ankle fractures)
[1765] DGH and MIU torus fractures: NG38 compliance 44% → 62% combined, fewer fracture clinic follow-ups (posters, email and teaching)
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic list plus PACS
pass: No wrist X-ray taken at the cast-removal visit, OR an X-ray taken with a documented clinical reason (for example tenderness, deformity, new symptoms).
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In adults with a scaphoid fracture seen on plain X-ray, was a CT scan done to measure displacement?
why: Plain films under-estimate displacement; >2 mm changes treatment to fixation. Corpus scaphoid audits focus on MRI for occult fractures ([1259], [1223], [1743]); none measured CT for visible fractures.

standard.source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Scaphoid fractures, standard 8 (BSSH, 2024; revision due 2027)
standard.wording: If a scaphoid fracture is visible on plain radiographs, CT scan should be performed to measure displacement accurately.

population: Include: adults (over 16) with an acute scaphoid fracture visible on initial radiographs. Exclude: tuberosity avulsion fractures, presentation more than 4 weeks after injury.
sample: 30–40 consecutive patients over the last 6–12 months.
data_source: PACS (radiographs, CT date); radiology reports; fracture/hand clinic letters.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

change: Add 'CT scaphoid (sagittal and coronal along scaphoid axis)' as an automatic request on the VFC scaphoid-fracture outcome, with the reconstruction protocol agreed with radiology.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 (or next 3 months for numbers), same template and sample size.
close_loop: Present at hand/T&O audit and radiology; if it works, keep the VFC auto-request and the CT protocol.
evidence: [1259] Dorset ED: patients with signs but normal films not sent for MRI 16% → 1% (scaphoid management protocol)
[1223] Southmead: MRI within 14 days 63% → 73% (limited-sequence MRI pathway)
[1743] Kings Mill DGH: clinic review within 7 days 68.5% (single cycle)
pass: A wrist/scaphoid CT performed after diagnosis (within 14 days of presentation) with displacement reported or measured.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: In adults with a scaphoid fracture treated non-operatively, was union confirmed on CT (or on X-ray at 6 months) before discharge from follow-up?
why: Missed non-union leads to collapse and arthritis. Scaphoid follow-up imaging is only a seed idea in the corpus ([666]); no detailed audit.

standard.source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Scaphoid fractures, standard 14 (BSSH, 2024; revision due 2027)
standard.wording: Patients should only be discharged once union is confirmed on CT (>50% of the fracture cross-sectional area) or by delayed radiographs at 6 months.

population: Include: adults with a confirmed scaphoid waist or distal pole fracture treated in a cast and discharged. Exclude: operative fixation, tuberosity avulsions, lost to follow-up.
sample: 30–40 consecutive discharged patients over the last 12 months.
data_source: Clinic letters (discharge date); PACS/radiology reports (CT union, 6-month films).

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
Secondary: standard 14 also requires this advice

change: A scaphoid discharge checklist in the clinic letter template: 'Union confirmed on: CT date __ / 6-month X-ray date __; non-union advice given'.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 (or 3 months), next 30–40 discharges, same template.
close_loop: Present at hand/T&O audit; if it works, keep the checklist in the clinic letter template.
evidence: [1259] Dorset: protocol cut time to MRI 37.6 → 11.4 days (system change; shows protocols work in scaphoid care)
[666] seed topic only: scaphoid follow-up imaging (not individually linked)
pass: Before the discharge date: a CT reporting union (>50% bridging), OR radiographs at ≥6 months after injury showing union.
area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

standard.wording: for closed injuries; green – next available clinic (real or virtual) within 72 hours

question: In patients with a hand bite that broke the skin, were antibiotics started on the day of first attendance?

standard.source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Human and animal bites to the hand (BSSH, 2021)
standard.wording: Antibiotics should be started as soon as possible after injury.

population: Include: human or animal bites to the hand or wrist with the dermis breached (including 'fight bites'). Exclude: superficial bites with no dermal breach.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months.

standard.source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Open fractures (BSSH, 2021)
standard.wording: Antibiotics should be stopped at 72 hours or after definitive closure whichever is the sooner, subject to clinical judgement.

population: Include: adults with an open fracture of the hand or digit (excluding tuft fractures) treated surgically. Exclude: established infection at presentation.

question: In adults with a new spinal column fracture confirmed on imaging, was the rest of the spine imaged?
why: Non-contiguous spinal fractures are common and easy to miss. No audit in corpus measured whole-spine imaging after a new fracture.

standard.wording: If a new spinal column fracture is confirmed, image the rest of the spinal column.

population: Include: adults (16 or over) with a new traumatic spinal column fracture. Exclude: pathological fractures from known metastases, patients who died before imaging.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months (radiology report search for 'fracture' with spine codes).
data_source: Radiology system/PACS (regions imaged and times); ED and T&O notes.

question: In adults with a spinal fracture managed non-operatively, did the notes state the fracture's stability and the brace or collar plan with its duration?
why: Unclear plans cause wrong brace use and repeat referrals. New BOAST (April 2025); no audit in corpus.

standard.source: BOAST Assessment of the Spine in the Trauma Patient (BOA, April 2025)
standard.wording: If a fracture is to be treated non-operatively, the decision-making team should specify the degree of stability of the fracture and details of the planned non-operative management, such as use of collar/ brace, including duration, care and changing procedures.

population: Include: adults with a traumatic cervical, thoracic or lumbar fracture treated non-operatively. Exclude: patients transferred for surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Spinal referral system advice (for example Referapatient); T&O and ward notes; discharge summary.

question: In adults with diabetes admitted under trauma and orthopaedics, was a documented foot examination (both feet) done within 24 hours of admission?
why: Orthopaedic inpatients with diabetes are at high risk of heel ulcers in bed and casts. No orthopaedic audit of admission foot checks in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE NG19 rec 1.3.3 (2015, guideline updated 2019)
standard.wording: For adults with diabetes, assess their risk of developing a diabetic foot problem at the following times: ... On any admission to hospital, and if there is any change in their status while they are in hospital.

population: Include: adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes admitted to a T&O ward (trauma or elective) staying ≥24 hours. Exclude: bilateral lower-limb amputees.
sample: 40 consecutive admissions over the last 1–2 months.
data_source: Ward nursing admission bundle; medical clerking; diabetes team notes.

question: In adults with a diabetic foot infection started on IV antibiotics, was the IV antibiotic reviewed within 48 hours?
why: Unreviewed IV antibiotics prolong stays and line use. Corpus diabetic foot audits look at sampling ([2388], [2386]); none at the 48-hour IV review.

standard.wording: If intravenous antibiotics are given, review by 48 hours and consider switching to oral antibiotics if possible.

population: Include: adults admitted under T&O, vascular or medicine with a diabetic foot infection started on IV antibiotics. Exclude: death or transfer within 48 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: EPMA/drug chart (first IV dose time, switch time); medical notes (review entry); microbiology results.

question: In adults with a diabetic foot ulcer seen by the orthopaedic or foot and ankle team, was ulcer severity recorded with SINBAD or the University of Texas system?
why: Without a standard score, change over time and referral urgency are unclear. No audit in corpus measured ulcer scoring; NICE also advises against Wagner.

standard.source: NICE NG19 rec 1.5.2 (2015)
standard.wording: Use a standardised system to document the severity of the foot ulcer, such as the SINBAD (Site, Ischaemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial Infection, Area and Depth) or the University of Texas classification system.

population: Include: adults with diabetes and an active foot ulcer reviewed by T&O (ward referral, fracture clinic or foot and ankle clinic). Exclude: ulcers already scored by the MDT foot service at the same visit.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Orthopaedic referral and clinic notes; ward review notes; podiatry records.
